interest: This file provides valuable historical insight into the transition from wartime economic mobilization to peacetime commodity governance, highlighting the intersection of raw material diplomacy, industrial reconversion, and post-war justice. It clearly illustrates the commercial friction between U.S. efforts to lower rubber prices using synthetic GR-S capacity and the urgent need of European colonial powers (Great Britain and the Netherlands) to maximize dollar exchange earnings from Southeast Asian rubber plantations to rebuild their domestic economies. Furthermore, the documents illuminate the complex forensic and administrative mechanisms developed to deal with looted property in occupied Japan, showing how joint British, Dutch, and American physical inspections of cargo markings and production dates were used to establish property rights and arbitrate restitution claims before the Far Eastern Commission.
overview: This State Department file (894.6176, spanning August 1945 through December 1946) details United States and Allied policy regarding natural, synthetic, and reclaimed rubber following the surrender of Japan. The collection documents high-level U.S. inter-agency discussions on post-war Far Eastern rubber price policy, efforts to establish competitive parity between synthetic GR-S and plantation rubber, and inquiries from private American manufacturers such as B.F. Goodrich regarding reparations claims against Japanese firms. A major portion consists of series documents from the Combined Rubber Committee evaluating quarterly requirements and allocating scarce global rubber supplies across Australia, New Zealand, Canada, South Africa, Denmark, Norway, Spain, and UNRRA. Finally, the file chronicles the allocation to the United States of 10,000 metric tons of natural rubber stockpiled in Japan, detailing inter-agency coordination between the State Department and the RFC Office of Rubber Reserve, as well as joint Anglo-American-Dutch port inspections to examine bale markings and production dates in order to substantiate restitution claims for rubber looted by Japan from Southeast Asia.

subfiles.about: Discussion between State Department and Rubber Development Corporation officials regarding procurement authority, international pricing negotiations, and synthetic versus natural rubber competition in the Far East.
subfiles.from: J. N. DuBarry, Commodities Division, Department of State
subfiles.summary: State Department officials met with representatives of the Rubber Development Corporation to consider post-war rubber price policy and purchasing authority under Section 5(d) of the RFC Act and the Reconversion Act. The participants discussed production costs of synthetic rubber (GR-S) and pre-war natural rubber prices, concluding that prices should remain moderate to avoid domestic inflation, protect consumers, and reestablish natural rubber in fair competition with synthetic alternatives. The group agreed that the State Department would lead future price negotiations with British, Dutch, French, and Thai authorities following an exploratory Rubber Study Group meeting in London. The meeting also addressed proposals to dispatch a U.S. industry mission to Malaya and the Netherlands East Indies, which the State Department opposed unless conducted as an official governmental advisory panel.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on Rubber Price Policy for the Far East

subfiles.about: Transmittal of a letter from The B.F. Goodrich Company concerning Japanese rubber machinery and reparations claims to the Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs.
subfiles.from: Ray Hicks, Office of the Publication Board, Department of Commerce
subfiles.summary: Ray Hicks of the Office of the Publication Board transmits an inquiry dated November 6, 1945, from Norm Keeling of The B.F. Goodrich Company to Edwin M. Martin in the State Department. Hicks explains that Martin's division was identified as the proper body to evaluate proposals regarding Japanese rubber assets and requests a copy of the Department's eventual reply for their files.
subfiles.title: Office Memorandum Regarding B.F. Goodrich Company Inquiry
subfiles.to: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Inquiry from The B.F. Goodrich Company concerning unpaid balances owed by Yokohama Rubber Company and the possibility of obtaining Japanese rubber machinery via reparations for relocation to China or New Zealand.
subfiles.from: Norm Keeling, Manager, Washington Office, International Division, The B.F. Goodrich Company
subfiles.summary: Norm Keeling of The B.F. Goodrich Company follows up on a conversation with Dow Harter concerning outstanding balances amounting to several hundred thousand dollars owed by the Yokohama Rubber Company of Japan. Keeling suggests that Harter contact Edwin Pauley or members of the Reparations Committee to advocate that Goodrich be permitted to acquire Japanese tire and tube machinery if Japanese manufacturing is discontinued. Goodrich proposes transferring such equipment to new company operations in either China or New Zealand.
subfiles.title: Letter from Norm Keeling to Dow Harter on Yokohama Rubber Company Balances and Japanese Rubber Machinery

subfiles.about: Statement of State Department policy regarding the absence of established machinery for private reparations claims against Japanese industrial assets.
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
keywords: Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.summary: Edwin M. Martin replies to Norm Keeling's referred letter concerning B.F. Goodrich's unpaid accounts with Yokohama Rubber Company and its interest in acquiring Japanese rubber machinery. Martin explains that no governmental machinery currently exists to receive or process claims by American citizens regarding reparations payments. He anticipates that an Inter-Allied Reparations Commission will eventually be formed, at which time the U.S. representative will invite American firms to declare their interest in Japanese assets designated for reparations.
subfiles.title: Letter from Edwin M. Martin to Norm Keeling on Reparations Policy and Japanese Assets
subfiles.to: Norm Keeling, Manager, Washington Office, International Division, The B.F. Goodrich Company

subfiles.about: Combined Rubber Committee note on the allocation to the United States of exportable rubber discovered in Japan and British conditions regarding pricing and provenance.
subfiles.from: Combined Rubber Committee
subfiles.summary: Document CRC-21 records the Combined Rubber Committee's agreement to allocate exportable rubber found in Japan to the United States following State Department representations. The British member consented on condition that the price matches prevailing Far Eastern market prices and that an investigation be conducted to determine the original ownership of the rubber. The note states that the price will not exceed standard Far Eastern rates and addresses questions regarding investigations into original ownership.
subfiles.title: Combined Rubber Committee Document CRC-21: Note on Allocation to the United States of Rubber Available in Japan

subfiles.about: Approval of a supplemental first-quarter allocation of 2,000 long tons of Malayan natural rubber to Canada.
subfiles.from: Combined Rubber Committee
subfiles.summary: Document CRC-22 addresses a request from the Canadian member for a supplemental allocation of 2,000 long tons of natural rubber due to low Canadian stock levels and extended shipping pipelines. The committee approved the transfer of 2,000 long tons from British Malayan availabilities previously assigned to the United Kingdom to meet Canada's immediate industrial needs.
subfiles.title: Combined Rubber Committee Document CRC-22: Note on Supplemental First Quarter Allocation to Canada

subfiles.about: Review of Australia's second-quarter rubber requirements, stock data, and application for liquid latex from Ceylon.
subfiles.from: Combined Rubber Committee
subfiles.summary: Document CRC-23 presents Australia's second-quarter requirement of 6,900 long tons of rubber, reflecting an industrial manufacturing program transitioning from 35 percent synthetic rubber usage to 100 percent natural rubber by late 1946. Australia also requested 60,000 gallons of liquid latex for sponge, footwear, gloves, and can-sealing manufacturing. Because Ceylon's monthly latex production was limited to 3,000 gallons, the committee recommended that available supplies be apportioned between Australia and New Zealand.
subfiles.title: Combined Rubber Committee Document CRC-23: Note on Second Quarter Requirements of Australia

subfiles.about: Statement of New Zealand's second-quarter rubber requirements, industrial usage breakdown, and request for Ceylon liquid latex.
subfiles.from: Combined Rubber Committee
subfiles.summary: Document CRC-24 outlines New Zealand's second-quarter allocation request for 660 long tons of natural rubber, which combines projected consumption of 540 tons and an unfulfilled first-quarter deficit of 120 tons. The required tonnage is earmarked for essential goods including cycle tires, milking rubber ware, gum boots, and camelback. The report also addresses New Zealand's bid for 6,000 gallons of Ceylon liquid latex, endorsing a proportional division of Ceylon's export surplus with Australia.
subfiles.title: Combined Rubber Committee Document CRC-24: Note on Second Quarter Requirements of New Zealand

subfiles.about: Assessment of South Africa's second-quarter rubber requirements and review of stock, consumption, and import statistics.
subfiles.from: Combined Rubber Committee
subfiles.summary: Document CRC-25 evaluates South Africa's formal second-quarter request for 1,800 long tons of natural rubber, to be drawn from Ceylon (1,300 tons) and India (500 tons). South African authorities expressed a preference for an additional 1,200 tons but refrained from requesting it due to overall supply limitations. The committee noted recent imports from British East Africa and awaited further statistical clarification requested by the British member.
subfiles.title: Combined Rubber Committee Document CRC-25: Note on Second Quarter Requirements of South Africa

subfiles.about: Detailed summary of Denmark's second-quarter requests for crude rubber, liquid latex for medical products, Butyl, and reclaimed rubber.
subfiles.from: Combined Rubber Committee
subfiles.summary: Document CRC-26 reviews Denmark's second-quarter rubber requirement of 900 long tons of crude rubber and 200 tons of reclaim. It includes excerpts from the Danish Legation emphasizing an urgent need for liquid latex to manufacture essential hospital, surgical, and infant sanitary supplies depleted during the German occupation. The report also conveys a Danish request for a 10-ton trial allocation of Butyl (GR-I) synthetic rubber to conduct industrial product tests.
subfiles.title: Combined Rubber Committee Document CRC-26: Note on Second Quarter Requirements of Denmark

subfiles.about: Review of Norway's second-quarter rubber allocations, increased tire factory capacity, and requests for natural rubber, latex, and Butyl.
subfiles.from: Combined Rubber Committee
subfiles.summary: Document CRC-27 presents an application by the Norwegian Purchasing Agency for a net second-quarter allocation of 510 long tons of natural rubber. The Norwegian representative explained that pre-war import averages underrepresented requirements due to tire plant expansions completed in 1939 that established an annual program of 2,600 tons. The document also details Norwegian requests for 9 long tons of liquid latex for dipped medical goods and 84 long tons of Butyl rubber for tube manufacturing.
subfiles.title: Combined Rubber Committee Document CRC-27: Note on Second Quarter Requirements of Norway

subfiles.about: Summary of Spain's annual rubber needs, syndicate procurement through Pirelli, and bilateral tire manufacturing agreements with Portugal.
subfiles.from: Combined Rubber Committee
subfiles.summary: Document CRC-28 conveys a report from the Commercial Counselor of the Spanish Embassy estimating Spain's annual requirements at 6,000 tons each of natural and synthetic rubber. The note details attempts by the Spanish Syndicate to procure 250 tons through Pirelli, appeals for compensation for missed 1945 quotas, and lists reclaim rubber needs. It also reports an arrangement with Portugal under which natural rubber imported from Portuguese African colonies would be manufactured into tires in Spain and returned to Portugal.
subfiles.title: Combined Rubber Committee Document CRC-28: Note on Second Quarter Requirements of Spain

subfiles.about: Presentation of an UNRRA request for 300 metric tons of natural liquid latex for medical rehabilitation in Byelorussia and Ukraine.
subfiles.from: Combined Rubber Committee
subfiles.summary: Document CRC-29 details a supplementary request from UNRRA for 300 metric tons of natural liquid latex, comprising 100 tons for Byelorussia and 200 tons for Ukraine to produce medical and surgical items. UNRRA withdrew its previous crude rubber bids for these Soviet republics in light of acute processing needs, requesting supply from the U.K. or U.S. Committee staff noted that U.K. second-quarter export availabilities amounted to only 65 long tons, making it impossible to satisfy more than a fraction of the request.
subfiles.title: Combined Rubber Committee Document CRC-29: Note on UNRRA Request for Second Quarter Allocation of Liquid Latex

subfiles.about: Confirmation of War Department intelligence indicating that 10,000 metric tons of natural rubber were available for export from Japan.
subfiles.from: William T. Phillips, Special Assistant to the Chief, International Resources Division, Department of State
subfiles.summary: William T. Phillips writes to Enid Baird of the War Production Board confirming a telephone conversation regarding rubber supplies in Japan. Phillips cites War Department cable Z-19456 of February 28, 1946, confirming that 10,000 metric tons of natural rubber in Tokyo were available for export. This notification provided official confirmation for U.S. allocation claims before the Combined Rubber Committee.
subfiles.title: Letter from William T. Phillips to Enid Baird Confirming Rubber Availability in Japan

subfiles.about: State Department request to the Office of Rubber Reserve to record identifying markings on Japanese rubber shipments to investigate possible looting.
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
keywords: Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.summary: Edwin M. Martin advises Richard Baybutt that the Combined Rubber Committee has allocated to the United States 10,000 tons of rubber from Japan, to be imported via the U.S. Commercial Company and transferred to the Office of Rubber Reserve. Martin states that allied nations wish to establish whether this rubber was looted by the Japanese from Southeast Asia. He requests that Rubber Reserve inspect all incoming shipments and maintain records of identifying markings that could be used to prove provenance.
subfiles.title: Letter from Edwin M. Martin to Richard Baybutt Requesting Inspection of Japanese Rubber Markings
subfiles.to: Richard Baybutt, Deputy Director, Office of Rubber Reserve, Reconstruction Finance Corporation

subfiles.about: Agreement by the Office of Rubber Reserve to instruct port agents to examine and record identifying marks on rubber arriving from Japan.
subfiles.from: Richard Baybutt, Deputy Director, Office of Rubber Reserve, Reconstruction Finance Corporation
subfiles.summary: Richard Baybutt acknowledges Edwin M. Martin's letter of April 18 regarding the 10,000-ton rubber allocation from Japan. Baybutt confirms that Rubber Reserve has instructed its agents to log all identifying markings on the rubber upon discharge to help determine whether it was looted. He adds that shipments are expected to arrive at U.S. ports in early June 1946, at which point the collected data will be forwarded to the State Department.
subfiles.title: Letter from Richard Baybutt to Edwin M. Martin Agreeing to Inspect Japanese Rubber Markings
subfiles.to: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: File record copy of the State Department's April 18, 1946 instructions to inspect incoming Japanese rubber for identifying markings.
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
keywords: Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.summary: This document is an internal Department of State file copy of the April 18, 1946 letter sent by Edwin M. Martin to Richard Baybutt of the Office of Rubber Reserve. It confirms the allocation of 10,000 tons of Japanese rubber to the United States through the U.S. Commercial Company and reiterates the requirement to document identifying marks on bales to evaluate foreign looting claims.
subfiles.title: File Copy of Letter from Edwin M. Martin to Richard Baybutt on Japanese Rubber Inspection
subfiles.to: Richard Baybutt, Deputy Director, Office of Rubber Reserve, Reconstruction Finance Corporation

subfiles.about: Internal memorandum discussing total Japanese rubber stockpiles, General MacArthur's export limitations, and Lend-Lease settlement restrictions.
subfiles.from: Harlan P. Bramble, International Resources Division, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Harlan P. Bramble reports on proposals raised regarding a 24,248-metric-ton rubber stockpile identified in Japan. Bramble notes that Roswell Whitman indicated General Douglas MacArthur had authorized the export of only 10,000 tons allocated to the United States, reserving the remainder for Japanese domestic industry. In addition, Ambrose Cramer of the Lend-Lease division advised that settlement could not be executed via Lend-Lease agreements because the cutoff date with the United Kingdom on December 6, 1945 precluded financing subsequent shipments.
subfiles.title: Internal Memorandum from Harlan P. Bramble to William T. Phillips on Japanese Rubber Stockpiles and Lend-Lease
subfiles.to: William T. Phillips, International Resources Division, Department of State

subfiles.about: State Department follow-up requesting a summary report on cargo markings and quantities of Japanese rubber received by the Office of Rubber Reserve.
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Associate Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
keywords: Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman follows up on April correspondence with Richard Baybutt regarding rubber brought from Japan by the U.S. Commercial Company. Whitman requests a comprehensive summary report detailing the quantities of rubber bearing various identifying marks delivered to Rubber Reserve as of September 30, 1946. The report is needed to verify the provenance of shipments and respond to allied inquiries.
subfiles.title: Letter from Roswell H. Whitman to Richard Baybutt Requesting Summary Markings Report
subfiles.to: Richard Baybutt, Deputy Director, Office of Rubber Reserve, Reconstruction Finance Corporation

subfiles.about: Request from the Department of Commerce for State Department review and political redaction of public reports on rubber conditions in liberated Asian territories.
subfiles.from: E. G. Holt, Rubber Advisor, Commodities Branch, Office of International Trade, Department of Commerce
subfiles.summary: E. G. Holt submits draft reports on post-war rubber conditions in territories liberated from Japanese occupation to Donald Kennedy for State Department review. Holt explains that commercial rubber firms have expressed keen interest in the reports, which Commerce has already screened to excise objectionable domestic material. He requests that State review the remaining text to eliminate any sensitive foreign policy wording before the documents are released to industry and the public.
subfiles.title: Letter from E. G. Holt to Donald Kennedy on Liberated Areas Rubber Reports
subfiles.to: Donald Kennedy, Director, International Resources Division, Department of State

subfiles.about: British Embassy request to inspect Japanese rubber imports for production dates in addition to origin markings to substantiate restitution claims for looted colonial assets.
subfiles.from: C. B. Wilson, Raw Materials Section, British Embassy
subfiles.summary: C. B. Wilson reviews the disposition of the 10,000 tons of rubber allocated from Japan, stating that joint British, Dutch, and American inspections in U.S. ports had already surveyed two-thirds of the cargo. Wilson announces that the British government intends to submit formal restitution claims before the Far Eastern Commission for rubber identified as having originated in British Far Eastern territories. To prove that the rubber was looted during Japanese military occupation rather than acquired through pre-war trade, he requests that U.S. inspectors attempt to determine the production date and age of the remaining rubber.
subfiles.title: Letter from C. B. Wilson to I. M. Paige on Restitution Claims and Rubber Age Determination
subfiles.to: I. M. Paige, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Acknowledgment of British Embassy representations regarding the feasibility of determining production dates of rubber imported from Japan.
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Associate Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
keywords: Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman acknowledges C. B. Wilson's letter of November 29 concerning the determination of production dates on rubber brought from Japan. Whitman reports that the State Department has referred the British proposal to the Reconstruction Finance Corporation's Office of Rubber Reserve to assess its practical feasibility. He promises to notify the British Embassy as soon as a operational determination is reached.
subfiles.title: Letter from Roswell H. Whitman to C. B. Wilson Acknowledging British Restitution Request
subfiles.to: C. B. Wilson, Raw Materials Section, British Embassy

subfiles.about: State Department endorsement of the British request to determine production dates of imported Japanese rubber and follow-up on the overdue summary markings report.
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Associate Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
keywords: Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman encloses C. B. Wilson's letter of November 29 and recommends that the Office of Rubber Reserve comply with the British request to determine the production dates of rubber imported from Japan. Whitman considers the request reasonable to facilitate upcoming restitution determinations by the Far Eastern Commission. He also inquires when Rubber Reserve will deliver the comprehensive cargo inspection report requested by the Department in late October.
subfiles.title: Letter from Roswell H. Whitman to Richard Baybutt Endorsing British Inspection Request
subfiles.to: Richard Baybutt, Deputy Director, Office of Rubber Reserve, Reconstruction Finance Corporation
